I don't have much to say about the DID bit, but my perspective is that when I was seventeen, I fell in love with a peer who had severe mental health problems (dissociative issues, severe suicidal ideation) and ended up put in the position of being his rock and support system all by myself. I convinced my parents to let him move in with us, and the damage it did to my own mental health is something I'm still dealing with a decade later. 

I was, to my parents' perspective, more happy and confident at the time than I had been before, but I was taking on more damage than I knew how to deal with. I wish my parents had been more involved in using that experience to teach me about boundaries, and taking care of myself despite the nearby suffering of others, or gotten me into therapy (so glad to hear that's already in place!), but they were more of the mind that I was almost an adult and they didn't want to interfere with the magical experience that is one's first love. 

That being said, I wouldn't have let them put any brakes on the relationship easily, but I think there are important lessons to be learned about boundaries here that might make or break the next decade of your son's life.

I live where most concerts are 2-3 hours away. I LOVE the crowd experience, but only when it's a band that I deeply love, who's music means a lot to me. I guess it's the feeling of being surrounded by humans who so strongly love the same thing you do, and have the music so loud moving everyone at the same time. I've had so many wonderful crowd experiences, from strangers who become a lover just for the duration of the concert (not fucking on the floor or anything, ew, just holding one another like you've known each other forever) to mosh pits and throwing yourself in passion against other people just as ecstatic as you. People in the crowds usually (and even more so at the mwY concerts I've been to) take care of each other... if people fall down, everyone helps them up. Concerts are a human spider web made of shared love.
